name: SHACKLETON RIM — the lunar south pole
blurb: A real 13 degree rim grade, from LOLA polar topography at 5 m/px — the finest lunar terrain published anywhere. Steep enough that the ankle runs out of dorsiflexion before the solver runs out of ideas.

meta.site: Shackleton Crater rim — lunar south pole
meta.citation: NASA LRO LOLA polar GDR, south of 87.5 S, 5 m/px
meta.grid: azimuthal equidistant about the site, resampled bilinear, long axis on bearing 206 deg
meta.resolution_note: source product is 5 m/px; this 1024x512 grid at 1.25 m/px spans 256 x 128 source posts and is a 4x bilinear resampling of them — interpolation, not added detail
meta.layout: row-major, +x along the traverse, +y to its left
meta.note: Steep rim ascent. Best public lunar topography anywhere: 5 m/px.

lope.label: LOPE
lope.blurb: The gait the Apollo crews adopted within minutes on every mission. One foot at a time, airborne between every step — a walk whose double support has been replaced by flight.

bound.label: BOUND
bound.blurb: Both feet together, everything into the vertical. The robot is identical on all three bodies and pushes identically, so the whole difference in height and hang is the field.

trip.label: TRIP + RECOVER
trip.blurb: A caught toe, and the fall that follows. Toppling is a pendulum about the toe, so the time to go over scales as 1/sqrt(g): 0.93 s on Earth against 2.28 s on the Moon. That extra second and a third is what the Apollo crews used to get a hand down.
